question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-30, what is the legal effect of a traditional "mortgage" (as opposed to a security deed) executed in Georgia?
choice_a: A mortgage is only security for a debt and passes no title to the property; the borrower retains legal title and the lender holds a lien
choice_b: A mortgage automatically converts to a security deed after 30 days if unpaid
choice_c: A mortgage conveys full legal title to the lender exactly as a security deed does
choice_d: A mortgage is unenforceable in Georgia and may not be used to secure real estate debt
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-30 provides that "a mortgage in this state is only security for a debt and passes no title." This makes a true mortgage a lien-theory instrument in Georgia, in contrast to a security deed under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-60, which does pass title to the lender as grantee.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-31, what must a mortgage instrument contain to be valid in Georgia?
choice_a: It must be signed by a notary public who is also a licensed attorney
choice_b: It must clearly indicate the creation of a lien, specify the debt it secures, and specify the property on which it takes effect
choice_c: It must include the borrower's Social Security number and date of birth
choice_d: It must be recorded within 24 hours of execution or it is automatically void
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-31 sets the formal content requirements for a valid Georgia mortgage: it must clearly indicate creation of a lien, specify the debt secured, and specify the property subject to it.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-33, what is required for a Georgia mortgage to be eligible for recording, and what effect does proper recording have?
choice_a: The mortgage need not be signed by the borrower at all if the lender records it
choice_b: Recording a mortgage in Georgia has no legal effect on subsequent purchasers
choice_c: The mortgage must be signed by the maker, attested by an officer as provided by law, and attested by one other witness; once properly recorded, it provides constructive notice to subsequent purchasers
choice_d: The mortgage must be attested by two officers and no witnesses to be recordable
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-33 requires a Georgia mortgage to be signed by the maker and attested by an officer plus one other witness; once recorded, it gives constructive notice to later purchasers of the property.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-162.2, how much advance written notice must a secured creditor generally give a debtor before initiating a nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure in Georgia?
choice_a: No advance notice is required beyond the newspaper advertisement itself
choice_b: At least 90 days before the proposed foreclosure sale
choice_c: At least 24 hours before the proposed foreclosure sale
choice_d: No later than 30 days before the date of the proposed foreclosure sale
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-162.2 requires the secured creditor to give the debtor written notice of the initiation of foreclosure proceedings no later than 30 days before the proposed foreclosure date.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-162.2, how must the pre-foreclosure notice be delivered to the debtor, and what must it contain?
choice_a: It must be sent by registered or certified mail, or statutory overnight delivery, return receipt requested, and must include the name, address, and telephone number of the individual or entity authorized to negotiate, amend, or modify the loan terms
choice_b: It may be delivered verbally by telephone with no written follow-up required
choice_c: It must be posted publicly on the courthouse steps only, with no direct communication to the debtor
choice_d: It must be delivered by a sheriff's deputy in person or it is invalid
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-162.2 requires delivery by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, return receipt requested, and requires the notice to identify a contact for loan modification negotiations -- though the statute does not obligate the creditor to actually modify the loan.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-162, if a foreclosure advertisement includes the property's street address, city, and ZIP code, how must that information be displayed?
choice_a: It must be printed in red ink
choice_b: It must be clearly set out in bold type
choice_c: It may be omitted entirely and is never required
choice_d: It must be underlined and italicized simultaneously
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-162 requires that when a foreclosure advertisement includes the street address, city, and ZIP code of the property, that information must be clearly set out in bold type.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-161, what must a lender do within 30 days after a Georgia foreclosure sale before it may pursue a deficiency judgment against the borrower?
choice_a: File a new deed of gift transferring the property to a third party
choice_b: Refund the borrower's entire down payment
choice_c: Report the sale to the judge of the superior court of the county where the land is located for confirmation and approval
choice_d: Obtain approval from the Georgia Real Estate Commission
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-161 requires the foreclosing party to report the sale to the superior court judge within 30 days for confirmation and approval before it may recover a deficiency judgment against the debtor.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-161, on what basis will a Georgia superior court judge confirm a foreclosure sale?
choice_a: Automatically, as a ministerial act with no substantive review of the sale price
choice_b: Only if the winning bidder is the original lender
choice_c: Only if the sale price exceeds the original purchase price of the property
choice_d: Only if satisfied by evidence that the property actually brought its true market value at the sale
explanation: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-161, the court requires evidence of the property's true market value and will not confirm the sale unless satisfied the property brought that value -- protecting the debtor from being subject to a deficiency judgment based on an undersold foreclosure.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-14-161, how much advance notice of the confirmation hearing must be given to the debtor?
choice_a: At least 5 days prior to the hearing
choice_b: At least 60 days prior to the hearing
choice_c: No notice to the debtor is required for the confirmation hearing
choice_d: At least 1 business day prior to the hearing
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-14-161 requires that notice of the confirmation hearing be given to the debtor at least 5 days before the hearing.

question: After a valid nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure has been completed in Georgia, does the foreclosed former owner generally have a statutory right to redeem the property by paying off the debt?
choice_a: Yes -- Georgia gives every foreclosed owner an automatic 12-month statutory redemption period
choice_b: No -- Georgia does not provide a general statutory post-sale right of redemption for real property; any equitable right to redeem generally exists only before the foreclosure sale is completed
choice_c: Yes -- Georgia gives every foreclosed owner an automatic 6-month statutory redemption period matching the tax sale redemption rules
choice_d: Yes -- but only for commercial property, never residential property
explanation: Unlike some states, Georgia does not provide a general post-sale statutory right of redemption for a foreclosed security deed or mortgage. A debtor's equitable right to redeem by paying the debt generally exists only up until the foreclosure sale is completed, consistent with Georgia's power-of-sale foreclosure procedure under O.C.G.A. §§ 44-14-160 et seq.
source_note: hedge: standard Georgia foreclosure practice; no statutory post-sale redemption provision identified in Title 44 Chapter 14

question: Conceptually, what is the intangible recording tax under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-61 assessed against?
choice_a: The annual property tax assessment of the secured real estate
choice_b: The gross sales commission earned by the listing broker on the transaction
choice_c: The face amount of a long-term note secured by real property in Georgia, at the time the security instrument is recorded
choice_d: The borrower's total household income for the year of closing
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-61 imposes an intangible recording tax on the face amount of long-term notes secured by real estate, collected when the security instrument is recorded, at $1.50 per $500 (or fraction thereof).

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 48-6-60(3), what distinguishes a "long-term note secured by real estate" (subject to the intangible recording tax) from a short-term note?
choice_a: A long-term note is any note with an interest rate above 6%
choice_b: A long-term note is any note in an original principal amount over $1,000,000
choice_c: A long-term note is defined solely by whether it is secured by commercial, rather than residential, property
choice_d: A long-term note is one in which any part of the principal falls due more than three years from the date of the note or the date of the instrument securing it
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-60(3) defines a long-term note secured by real estate as one where any part of the principal falls due more than three years after the date of the note (or of the securing instrument) -- notes maturing entirely within three years fall outside that long-term definition.

question: Under Georgia's usury statute, O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2, what is the maximum simple interest rate that may generally be charged on a loan of $3,000 or less?
choice_a: 16% per annum simple interest
choice_b: There is no cap at all on loans of any size in Georgia
choice_c: 8% per annum simple interest
choice_d: 36% per annum simple interest
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2 caps the interest rate on loans of $3,000 or less at 16% per annum simple interest, absent a more specific statute governing that loan type.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2, is there a statutory usury ceiling on the interest rate the parties may contract for on a loan greater than $3,000 in Georgia?
choice_a: Yes -- all loans in Georgia, regardless of size, are capped at 16% per annum
choice_b: No -- for loans above $3,000, the parties may establish by written contract any rate of interest they agree to
choice_c: Yes -- loans above $3,000 are capped at exactly 10% per annum
choice_d: Yes -- loans above $3,000 are capped at the federal discount rate plus 2%
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2 removes the usury ceiling for loans above $3,000, allowing the parties to contract freely for any interest rate, unlike the 16% cap that applies to loans of $3,000 or less.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2, what is the default "legal rate" of interest in Georgia when parties have no written contract specifying a rate?
choice_a: 0% -- interest cannot accrue without an express written contract
choice_b: 16% per annum simple interest, the same as the small-loan cap
choice_c: 7% per annum simple interest
choice_d: 10% per annum simple interest
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2 sets the default "legal rate" of interest, absent a written contract specifying a different rate, at 7% per annum simple interest.

question: Under the Georgia Fair Lending Act (O.C.G.A. § 7-6A-2), what points-and-fees threshold helps classify a home loan of $20,000 or more as a "high-cost home loan"?
choice_a: Total points and fees exceeding 25% of the total loan amount
choice_b: Any origination fee at all, regardless of amount
choice_c: Total points and fees exceeding 1% of the total loan amount
choice_d: Total points and fees (excluding up to two bona fide discount points) exceeding 5% of the total loan amount
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 7-6A-2 sets a high-cost home loan points-and-fees threshold, for loans of $20,000 or more, at total points and fees exceeding 5% of the loan amount (excluding up to two bona fide discount points).

question: Under the Georgia Fair Lending Act, what is the alternative basis (besides the points-and-fees test) for classifying a loan as a "high-cost home loan"?
choice_a: The loan's annual percentage rate equals or exceeds the trigger rate established under the federal Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act (HOEPA) and corresponding Federal Reserve regulations
choice_b: The borrower's credit score is below 620, regardless of the loan's rate or fees
choice_c: The loan term exceeds 15 years
choice_d: The property is located outside a metropolitan statistical area
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 7-6A-2 provides that a loan is also classified as "high-cost" if its APR equals or exceeds the HOEPA trigger rate under federal law, as an alternative to the points-and-fees threshold.

question: Under the Georgia Residential Mortgage Act (O.C.G.A. § 7-1-1000 et seq.), how is a "mortgage broker" generally distinguished from a "mortgage lender"?
choice_a: There is no legal distinction; the terms are fully interchangeable under Georgia law
choice_b: A mortgage broker solicits, processes, places, or negotiates mortgage loans for others, while a mortgage lender makes, originates, underwrites, holds, or purchases mortgage loans
choice_c: A mortgage broker may only work on commercial loans, while a mortgage lender may only work on residential loans
choice_d: A mortgage broker must be a Georgia-licensed attorney, while a mortgage lender need not be
explanation: The Georgia Residential Mortgage Act's definitions distinguish a mortgage broker (who solicits, processes, places, or negotiates loans for others) from a mortgage lender (who makes, originates, underwrites, holds, or purchases mortgage loans).

question: Under the Georgia Residential Mortgage Act, through what national system do mortgage loan originators register and obtain their license?
choice_a: The Georgia Real Estate Commission's separate, state-only licensing portal, unconnected to any national system
choice_b: The Federal Housing Finance Agency's loan originator database
choice_c: The Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS)
choice_d: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's direct federal licensing office
explanation: The Georgia Residential Mortgage Act incorporates the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS) for registering and licensing mortgage loan originators, consistent with the federal SAFE Act framework.

question: Under the Georgia Residential Mortgage Fraud statute (O.C.G.A. § 16-8-102), what is a core element of the crime of residential mortgage fraud?
choice_a: Simply having a credit score below a lender's minimum requirement
choice_b: Failing to make a mortgage payment on time
choice_c: Refinancing a loan more than once in a 12-month period
choice_d: Knowingly making a deliberate misstatement, misrepresentation, or omission during the mortgage lending process with the intent to deceive a lender or borrower
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 16-8-102 criminalizes knowingly making a deliberate misstatement, misrepresentation, or omission during the mortgage lending process with intent to deceive, among other listed acts such as knowingly receiving proceeds from a fraudulent closing or filing false loan documents.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 16-8-102, does the Georgia Residential Mortgage Fraud statute apply to information that is legally required to be disclosed under other mortgage regulations?
choice_a: No -- the statute explicitly excludes information disclosed as required by federal or state mortgage lending law, as well as documents filed to correct bona fide clerical errors
choice_b: Yes -- any disclosure at all, even one required by federal law, can independently trigger criminal liability
choice_c: The statute is silent on the issue and courts have never addressed it
choice_d: It applies only to disclosures made by real estate licensees, never by lenders
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 16-8-102 carves out legally required disclosures made in compliance with applicable mortgage lending regulations, and documents filed solely to correct clerical errors, from criminal liability under the statute.

question: Under Georgia's recording statute, O.C.G.A. § 44-2-1, what happens to a prior deed or lien on real property that was never recorded, if a later purchaser or creditor records their own competing interest first without notice of the earlier one?
choice_a: The prior unrecorded deed or lien always keeps priority regardless of recording, because Georgia is a pure "race" state that ignores notice entirely
choice_b: The prior unrecorded deed or lien loses its priority to the later, properly recorded interest, since Georgia follows a race-notice recording system
choice_c: Recording has no legal effect on priority disputes in Georgia; only the date of the underlying debt matters
choice_d: The later recorded interest is automatically void as a matter of law
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-2-1 establishes that a prior unrecorded deed loses priority to a subsequently recorded deed from the same source when the later purchaser takes without notice of the earlier, unrecorded interest -- a race-notice recording rule.

question: What is a defining feature of a USDA Rural Development guaranteed home loan?
choice_a: It is available only in major metropolitan downtown areas
choice_b: It requires a minimum 20% down payment in every case
choice_c: It is generally available for eligible low- to moderate-income borrowers purchasing in designated rural areas, often with no down payment required, subject to income limits and a guarantee fee
choice_d: It is guaranteed by the Federal Reserve rather than the U.S. Department of Agriculture
explanation: USDA-guaranteed loans support eligible rural and moderate-income homebuyers, typically requiring no down payment, subject to household income limits, property-location eligibility, and an upfront/annual guarantee fee -- distinguishing it from FHA and VA financing.

question: Under the Truth in Lending Act (Regulation Z), what right generally applies when a borrower refinances a loan secured by their primary residence with a new lender (not a purchase-money loan)?
choice_a: An unlimited right to cancel the loan at any time before it is paid off
choice_b: A right of rescission that applies equally to purchase-money mortgages used to buy the home
choice_c: No cancellation right of any kind applies to any residential mortgage transaction
choice_d: A 3-business-day right of rescission, allowing the borrower to cancel the refinance transaction
explanation: TILA/Regulation Z generally gives borrowers a 3-business-day right to rescind a non-purchase-money refinance of their principal residence; this rescission right does not apply to purchase-money mortgages.

question: How does the Annual Percentage Rate (APR) disclosed under Truth in Lending generally differ from a loan's stated note (interest) rate?
choice_a: APR reflects the total cost of credit expressed as a yearly rate, incorporating certain finance charges such as points and fees in addition to the note rate, so it is typically higher than the note rate alone
choice_b: APR and the note rate are always identical numbers by definition
choice_c: APR reflects only the note rate with all fees excluded
choice_d: APR is set by the borrower's state government and has nothing to do with the loan's finance charges
explanation: APR is a broader cost-of-credit measure than the bare note rate because it factors in certain finance charges (e.g., points, some fees) spread over the loan term, generally making it higher than the note rate alone.

question: What does the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) generally prohibit in connection with mortgage lending?
choice_a: It prohibits lenders from charging any interest at all
choice_b: Discrimination against a credit applicant on the basis of characteristics such as race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, or age (among other protected bases), and it requires notice of the reasons for adverse credit decisions
choice_c: It prohibits lenders from ever declining a loan application for any reason
choice_d: It only applies to commercial loans, never to residential mortgage lending
explanation: ECOA prohibits credit discrimination based on protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, and age, and requires lenders to notify applicants of the specific reasons for an adverse action.

question: What is the general purpose of the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA)?
choice_a: It sets the maximum interest rate any lender may charge nationwide
choice_b: It requires every borrower to disclose their tax returns to their real estate agent
choice_c: It requires many mortgage lenders to collect, report, and publicly disclose data about mortgage applications and originations, helping regulators and the public monitor for discriminatory or otherwise unfair lending patterns
choice_d: It creates the federal deposit insurance fund for mortgage lenders
explanation: HMDA requires covered lenders to compile and publicly report data on mortgage applications and originations, supporting fair-lending monitoring and community-reinvestment analysis.

question: What did the federal SAFE Mortgage Licensing Act generally require of the states?
choice_a: That states abolish all mortgage loan originator licensing requirements
choice_b: That only federally chartered banks may originate residential mortgage loans
choice_c: That mortgage loan originators must also hold an active real estate broker's license
choice_d: That states establish minimum licensing and registration standards for mortgage loan originators, coordinated through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS)
explanation: The federal SAFE Act required states to adopt minimum licensing and registration standards for mortgage loan originators, implemented nationally through the NMLS -- the framework Georgia implements through its own Residential Mortgage Act.

question: What does the federal Ability-to-Repay rule (adopted under the Dodd-Frank Act) generally require of mortgage lenders?
choice_a: A reasonable, good-faith determination, based on verified information, that the borrower has a reasonable ability to repay the loan according to its terms
choice_b: A guarantee that the borrower will never default under any circumstances
choice_c: That every loan be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac within 90 days of closing
choice_d: That the lender waive all income verification for loans under $200,000
explanation: The Ability-to-Repay rule requires lenders to make a reasonable, good-faith, documented determination that a borrower can repay the mortgage, based on verified income, assets, debts, and other underwriting factors.

question: What is a general characteristic of a "Qualified Mortgage" (QM) under federal mortgage rules?
choice_a: It is a loan type reserved exclusively for second homes and investment property
choice_b: It generally provides the lender a degree of legal protection for complying with the Ability-to-Repay rule and typically excludes risky features such as negative amortization, interest-only payments, and most balloon payments, while limiting points and fees
choice_c: It is any loan with an adjustable rate reset every 30 days
choice_d: It guarantees the borrower a below-market fixed interest rate for the life of the loan
explanation: A Qualified Mortgage generally gives lenders a presumption of Ability-to-Repay compliance, and typically excludes higher-risk features (negative amortization, interest-only payments, most balloon terms) while capping points and fees.

question: Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act (HOPA), when does private mortgage insurance (PMI) on a qualifying conventional loan generally terminate automatically?
choice_a: PMI never terminates automatically under any circumstances and must always be separately requested
choice_b: Automatically, the day the loan closes, regardless of the down payment made
choice_c: Automatically, when the loan balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value of the property, based on the original amortization schedule (assuming the borrower is current)
choice_d: Automatically, once the borrower has made a single on-time payment
explanation: HOPA generally requires automatic termination of PMI on qualifying loans once the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the property's original value under the original amortization schedule, provided the borrower is current on payments.

question: Under HOPA, at what loan-to-value point may a borrower generally request cancellation of PMI on a qualifying loan (assuming good payment history)?
choice_a: A borrower may never request cancellation; only automatic termination at 78% is permitted
choice_b: At 95% loan-to-value, immediately after closing
choice_c: Only after the loan has been fully paid off
choice_d: When the loan balance reaches 80% of the original property value, the borrower may request cancellation
explanation: HOPA allows a borrower with good payment history to request PMI cancellation once the loan balance reaches 80% of the property's original value, ahead of the automatic 78% termination point.

question: What is a "discount point" in residential mortgage lending?
choice_a: A fee equal to 1% of the loan amount, paid by the borrower at closing in exchange for a reduced interest rate on the loan
choice_b: A penalty charged only when a borrower misses a payment
choice_c: A government rebate paid to first-time homebuyers
choice_d: A fee equal to 1% of the purchase price, unrelated to the loan amount
explanation: A discount point equals 1% of the loan amount and is paid upfront to "buy down" the interest rate, reducing the borrower's ongoing monthly payment in exchange for a higher closing cost.

question: How does a loan origination fee generally differ in purpose from discount points?
choice_a: They are legally identical and always charged at the same percentage
choice_b: An origination fee compensates the lender for the costs of processing and underwriting the loan application, while discount points are prepaid interest paid to reduce the loan's interest rate
choice_c: An origination fee is refunded at closing, while discount points are never refundable
choice_d: Discount points compensate the lender for underwriting costs, while the origination fee reduces the interest rate
explanation: The origination fee covers the lender's cost of processing/underwriting the loan, while discount points are a separate, optional prepayment of interest used to lower the note rate -- distinct charges serving different purposes even though both are often expressed as a percentage of the loan amount.

question: What does the "front-end" (housing expense) qualifying ratio generally measure in mortgage underwriting?
choice_a: The borrower's total household debt divided by their net (after-tax) monthly income
choice_b: The purchase price of the home divided by the borrower's annual income
choice_c: The borrower's proposed monthly housing payment (principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and applicable HOA dues) divided by the borrower's gross monthly income
choice_d: The down payment amount divided by the loan amount
explanation: The front-end (housing) ratio is the borrower's proposed total housing payment (PITI, plus HOA dues where applicable) divided by gross monthly income, used by underwriters to gauge housing-payment affordability.

question: What does the "back-end" (debt-to-income, or DTI) qualifying ratio generally measure in mortgage underwriting?
choice_a: Only the borrower's credit card balances divided by their net worth
choice_b: The lender's total loan portfolio risk divided by its total assets
choice_c: The borrower's housing payment alone, excluding all other debts, divided by gross monthly income
choice_d: The borrower's total monthly debt obligations, including the proposed housing payment plus other recurring debts, divided by the borrower's gross monthly income
explanation: The back-end (DTI) ratio adds the proposed housing payment to the borrower's other recurring monthly debts (e.g., car loans, student loans, credit cards) and divides that total by gross monthly income, giving a broader affordability measure than the front-end ratio alone.

question: How does a "wraparound" mortgage generally function?
choice_a: A new junior loan is created that includes (wraps) the balance of an existing underlying loan; the borrower makes payments to the wraparound lender, who in turn continues making payments on the original underlying loan
choice_b: It automatically pays off and cancels any existing underlying loan on the property at origination
choice_c: It requires the original underlying lender to formally release the original loan before closing
choice_d: It can only be used for loans that are already paid off in full
explanation: A wraparound mortgage is a form of junior seller/lender financing that "wraps" around an existing loan the underlying loan is not paid off; the wrap lender collects payments from the new borrower and continues servicing the original loan out of those proceeds.

question: As a general national doctrine, how is a purchase-money mortgage (a loan used to fund the purchase of the very property that secures it) often treated in terms of lien priority?
choice_a: It is always automatically subordinate to every other lien on the buyer's other property
choice_b: It is often treated as having priority over other liens or claims against the buyer that existed before the purchase, even though it is recorded at essentially the same time as the deed conveying title
choice_c: It receives no special priority treatment of any kind under any circumstances
choice_d: It automatically takes priority over property taxes assessed after closing
explanation: Purchase-money mortgages are commonly given special priority treatment under general real estate finance doctrine, since the loan enabled the buyer to acquire the property in the first place -- often outranking other judgment liens against the buyer that would otherwise attach at the moment of purchase.

question: What does a "subordination agreement" generally accomplish between lienholders?
choice_a: It permanently extinguishes the subordinated lien
choice_b: It automatically raises the subordinated lien to first priority
choice_c: It allows a lienholder to voluntarily agree that its lien will rank behind (be subordinate to) another lien in priority, even though the subordinating lien might otherwise have priority by recording date
choice_d: It transfers ownership of the underlying debt to a new creditor
explanation: A subordination agreement lets a lienholder voluntarily step back in priority behind another lien -- commonly used, for example, when a borrower refinances a first mortgage and needs an existing second mortgage holder to remain in second position behind the new first loan.

question: What distinguishes a "package mortgage" from a typical real estate loan?
choice_a: It combines two entirely separate parcels of real estate under a single loan with no personal property involved
choice_b: It is a loan that can never be secured by anything other than raw land
choice_c: It automatically includes a life insurance policy on the borrower as additional collateral
choice_d: It is secured by both the real property and certain items of personal property (such as built-in appliances or furnishings) included in the sale
explanation: A package mortgage secures both real property and specified items of personal property (e.g., appliances, furnishings) conveyed with the home, packaging real and personal property together as collateral for a single loan.

question: What is a "blanket mortgage" with a release clause typically used for?
choice_a: Financing that covers more than one parcel of real property under a single loan, with a release clause allowing individual parcels to be released from the lien as an allocated portion of the debt is paid off
choice_b: A loan that can only ever cover a single condominium unit
choice_c: A loan that automatically forgives the entire balance once any one parcel is sold
choice_d: A short-term loan used exclusively for personal, non-real-estate debts
explanation: A blanket mortgage secures multiple parcels (common in subdivision or builder financing), and its release clause lets individual parcels be released from the lien once a proportional part of the debt tied to that parcel has been paid.

question: What is a distinguishing feature of an open-end mortgage (such as a home equity line of credit, or HELOC)?
choice_a: It requires the full loan amount to be disbursed in a single lump sum at closing, with no further draws ever permitted
choice_b: It allows the borrower to draw additional future advances against the property, up to a stated maximum, generally retaining the lien priority of the original recorded instrument
choice_c: It has no maximum credit limit and can be drawn indefinitely without limit
choice_d: It converts automatically into a fixed-rate closed-end loan after the first draw
explanation: An open-end mortgage (e.g., a HELOC) lets the borrower draw, repay, and redraw funds up to a set credit limit secured by the same lien, generally preserving that lien's original recording priority for future advances made under it.

question: How are funds typically disbursed under a residential construction loan?
choice_a: As a single lump-sum payment to the borrower on day one, with no inspection of construction progress
choice_b: Only after the entire structure has already been fully completed and sold
choice_c: In a series of draws released as the project reaches defined stages of completion, rather than as a single lump sum at closing
choice_d: In equal monthly installments regardless of actual construction progress
explanation: Construction loans are typically disbursed in draws tied to inspected stages of completion (e.g., foundation, framing, drywall) to manage the lender's risk during the build, often converting to permanent financing once construction is finished.

question: What is a "bridge" (or "swing") loan generally used for in residential real estate?
choice_a: A 30-year fixed-rate loan used only for first-time homebuyers
choice_b: A permanent loan used to refinance a fully paid-off home
choice_c: A loan that can only be used to purchase raw, unimproved land
choice_d: Short-term financing that lets a homeowner tap the equity in their current home to fund the purchase of a new home before their current home has sold
explanation: A bridge (or swing) loan is short-term financing secured by a borrower's current home equity, used to "bridge" the gap and fund a new purchase before the existing home sale closes.

question: How does a temporary interest-rate buydown (such as a "2-1 buydown") generally work?
choice_a: Funds deposited at closing (often by the seller or builder) are used to temporarily subsidize the borrower's monthly payments at a reduced effective rate for an initial period, after which the payment reverts to the loan's actual note rate
choice_b: It permanently lowers the note rate for the full life of the loan with no future increase
choice_c: It requires the borrower to pay a higher rate for the first two years and a lower rate afterward
choice_d: It is a government subsidy program funded entirely by FHA with no cost to any private party
explanation: A temporary buydown (e.g., 2-1: 2% below note rate in year one, 1% below in year two) uses funds set aside at closing to subsidize the borrower's payments for a limited initial period, after which payments step up to the full note rate for the remainder of the loan.

question: What happens under "negative amortization" on a mortgage loan?
choice_a: The borrower pays extra principal each month, causing the balance to shrink faster than scheduled
choice_b: The borrower's payment is less than the interest accruing on the loan, so the unpaid interest is added to the principal balance, causing the loan balance to grow over time rather than shrink
choice_c: The lender forgives a portion of the principal balance every year automatically
choice_d: The interest rate is permanently fixed at 0% for the life of the loan
explanation: Negative amortization occurs when the scheduled payment does not cover the full interest accrued for the period; the shortfall is added to the principal, so the loan balance increases rather than amortizing down over time.

question: What is a defining feature of an interest-only mortgage during its interest-only period?
choice_a: The borrower's payment covers only principal, with all interest deferred until the loan matures
choice_b: The loan balance is automatically reduced to zero at the end of the interest-only period with no further borrower action
choice_c: The borrower's payment covers only the interest accrued for the period, so the principal balance does not decrease during that time
choice_d: The interest rate resets to 0% once the interest-only period ends
explanation: During the interest-only period, the borrower's payment covers accrued interest only, so the principal balance remains unchanged until the loan begins to amortize (or reaches a scheduled balloon or rate-reset event).

question: How does a formally lender-approved loan "assumption" generally differ from a buyer purchasing a property "subject to" the existing loan?
choice_a: The two terms describe exactly the same transaction with no legal distinction whatsoever
choice_b: In a formal assumption, the original borrower always remains liable and the new buyer is never liable
choice_c: A "subject to" purchase always requires the lender's prior written approval, just like a formal assumption
choice_d: In a formal assumption, the lender approves the new buyer and the new buyer becomes personally liable on the loan (often releasing the original borrower); in a "subject to" purchase, the buyer takes title and makes payments without lender approval, and the original borrower typically remains personally liable on the note
explanation: A qualifying, lender-approved assumption shifts personal liability to the new borrower (with lender underwriting); a "subject to" purchase involves no lender approval, so the original borrower generally remains on the note even though the new buyer is now making the payments and holding title -- a structure a due-on-sale clause could otherwise prevent absent lender consent.

question: In a typical fully amortizing fixed-rate mortgage, how does the composition of the level monthly payment (between interest and principal) generally change over the life of the loan?
choice_a: In the early years, a larger share of each payment goes to interest and a smaller share to principal; as the loan matures, the interest share shrinks and the principal share grows, even though the total payment stays the same
choice_b: The interest and principal portions of every payment are always exactly equal, from the first payment to the last
choice_c: The principal portion is largest in the early years and steadily shrinks to nearly zero by the end of the term
choice_d: The interest portion is fixed as a flat dollar amount for the entire loan term
explanation: Because interest is charged on the outstanding balance, early payments on a level-payment amortizing loan are weighted heavily toward interest; as the balance shrinks, later payments are weighted increasingly toward principal, even though the total payment amount does not change.

question: What is the general purpose of a mortgage escrow (impound) account?
choice_a: It is a fund the borrower may withdraw from at any time for personal expenses unrelated to the property
choice_b: The lender or servicer collects roughly one-twelfth of the borrower's estimated annual property taxes and homeowners insurance premium with each monthly payment, holding those funds to pay the tax and insurance bills when they come due
choice_c: It replaces the need for the borrower to ever obtain homeowners insurance
choice_d: It is used exclusively to prepay principal ahead of the amortization schedule
explanation: An escrow (impound) account lets the servicer collect monthly installments toward the borrower's annual property tax and insurance obligations, then pay those bills directly when due, reducing the risk of a lapse in coverage or a tax lien.

question: Under federal mortgage servicing rules, what protection generally applies to a borrower when their loan's servicing rights are transferred to a new servicer?
choice_a: The borrower's interest rate automatically resets to the current market rate upon any servicing transfer
choice_b: The loan balance is automatically forgiven whenever servicing is transferred
choice_c: The borrower must generally be given advance notice of the transfer, and there is a grace period during which a payment sent to the prior (wrong) servicer cannot be treated as late
choice_d: No notice of any kind is required when servicing is transferred, and payments to the wrong servicer are simply forfeited
explanation: Federal servicing-transfer rules require advance notice to the borrower and a grace period protecting the borrower from late fees or adverse credit reporting if a payment is mistakenly sent to the prior servicer shortly after a transfer.

question: As a general national concept (distinct from Georgia's own nonjudicial procedure), what characterizes a "judicial foreclosure"?
choice_a: It is a foreclosure that can be completed entirely without any lender action, initiated automatically by the county
choice_b: It refers to a foreclosure that occurs only through a private auction with no court or government involvement of any kind
choice_c: It is simply another name for a nonjudicial power-of-sale foreclosure
choice_d: The lender must file a lawsuit in court and obtain a court judgment and order of sale before the secured property can be sold to satisfy the debt
explanation: A judicial foreclosure requires the lender to sue in court and obtain a judgment (and typically a court-ordered sale) before the property can be sold -- a more time-consuming process than the nonjudicial power-of-sale procedure Georgia primarily uses.

question: Using a standard fully amortizing fixed-rate mortgage payment calculation, what is the monthly principal-and-interest (P&I) payment on a 30-year loan of $200,000 at a 6% annual interest rate?
explanation: Using the standard amortization formula (M = P x [i(1+i)^n] / [(1+i)^n - 1], where i is the monthly rate and n is the number of monthly payments), a 30-year, $200,000 loan at 6% amortizes to a monthly P&I payment of approximately $1,199.10. (Simply dividing annual interest by 12 -- $1,000 -- ignores the principal repayment component and understates the true payment.)
